ABHINAVA'S ORIGINAL EXTENSIONS: WHAT THE IPVV ADDS BEYOND THE IPK

The epistemology of action, the sphurattā, the parā-vāk, and the māheśvarya — the four regions only the commentary develops

  • 026-08-11. A companion to the Abhinava-vs-Utpaladeva essay. Where that essay isolated the
  • entifications (vimarśa = parā-vāk = sphurattā = māheśvarya), this essay expounds the four regions
  • Abhinava's original contribution — the bodies of doctrine that the IPK leaves undeveloped and that
  • e IPVV builds into a complete metaphysics. These are the territory the essay-3 razor calls "where the
  • VV goes further than both IPK and Ratié."*

1. The epistemology of action (the kriyādhikāra, V3A–I)

  • e IPK states the powers; it does not develop a theory of action. Abhinava devotes a whole adhikāra to
  • . This is Abhinava's largest original region.

1.1 Action as the will (V3A)

  • e kriyādhikāra opens the parallel: having established the power of knowledge, now the power of action.
  • d it confronts the paradox at the heart of the system: the Lord is beyond time and sequence, yet
  • nifests a world shot through with sequence. The answer is the mirror — a mirror bears countless
  • flections without ceasing to be one; so the timeless manifests order precisely because it is one.
"He bows to Śiva, who, though free of sequence, manifests manifold sequences." (V3A)
  • e action-support (kriyāśraya): the one that acts is one, and it is because it is one and undivided
  • at it can show sequence at all.

1.2 The action-cognitions as bhedābheda (V3B)

  • e action-cognitions (of action, relation, universal, substance, direction, time) are both one and
  • ny — "this is the very same body" (V3B). The distinction-and-non-distinction vimarśa is Abhinava's
  • swer to how the one appears as many without losing its unity.

1.3 Causality as the conscious knower's agency (V3G)

  • e deepest claim of the kriyādhikāra:
"The essence of cause and effect is nothing but the relation of agent and object of action.
Causality, in the end, is the agency of a conscious knower." (V3G)
  • e inert cannot be a cause — the seed cannot endow the sprout with being (V3G). The real cause is
  • nsciousness, the free will that shapes the effect. This is a full metaphysics of causation, which the
  • K does not develop.

1.4 Inference across knowers (V3H)

  • e Vijñānavādin's objection — how can you infer the fire from the smoke if cause and effect are only
  • lations between private appearances? — is answered: the Lord creates the appearances for all the
  • owers at once, as one, so the pervasion holds across streams (V3H).

1.5 The will as cause, agent, and action (V3I)

  • e crown of the kriyādhikāra:
"The cause does not cause, the agent does not act, the action does not move — all three are the one
will, by which the Lord, wishing to stand, becomes the world." (V3I)
  • d against the Advaita's "un-explainable ignorance," Abhinava argues the difference is real: "even
  • ahman with ignorance is [admitted by some], so this is not an absolute monism either" (V3I).
  • What this region contributes.** A complete epistemology and metaphysics of action — action = the
  • ll, causality = the knower's agency, inference across knowers by the one creation, and the
  • futation of the monist's "ignorance." None of this is in the IPK as a developed theory. It is
  • hinava's.

2. The sphurattā: the throbbing as the felt essence (V2I)

  • e IPK states the reflexivity-claim; Abhinava gives it a dynamic face — the throbbing.
"The throbbing (sphurattā) — the very pulsing of the manifestation — is the great being
(mahāsattā), undivided by place and time, the heart of the param-Lord." (kārikā 14, V2I)
  • e sphurattā is the same as the spanda, the wave (ūrmi), the eternal being. The self-aware
  • nifestation is not static; it is a pulsing, an ongoing act of self-articulation.
  • Why this is original.** Utpaladeva's reflexivity-claim is static (the essence of light is reflective
  • areness); Abhinava's sphurattā makes it dynamic, temporal, felt. This is where the recognition-thesis
  • d the felt meet: the pulse of self-awareness is the felt beat of being, "the heart of the
  • ram-Lord."
  • The systematic gain.** The sphurattā connects the Pratyabhijñā to the Spanda school (the pulsation),
  • d it gives the felt register (camatkāra) its home: the throbbing is the felt self-presence, the beat
  • the recognition.

3. The parā-vāk: the Word as the self-grasp (V2H/V2I)

  • e second identification: the reflexivity-claim is the supreme Word.
"This self-knowing is the parā-vāk, the supreme speech, from which all the lower levels of speech
(the madhyamā, the vaikharī) descend." (V2H)
  • Why this is original.** Utpaladeva's reflexivity-claim is about light; Abhinava identifies it with
  • e Word. Language is not an instrument consciousness uses; it is the very form the self-grasp takes.
  • e word-joined "I" is not a construction; it is the self's own articulation (V2L).
  • The systematic gain.** With the parā-vāk, Abhinava absorbs the entire philosophy of language — the
  • hoṭa, the grammarian's paśyantī, the vācaka-vācya structure — into the recognition-thesis. Speech is
  • t a second reality; it is consciousness's own self-grasp. The grammarian's separate supreme principle
  • dissolved (V2I): speech and the mind are only the ego's operation, quickened by the Lord's power.

4. The māheśvarya: the Lordship as the self-awareness (V2R/S)

  • e crowning identification, closing the jñānādhikāra:
"The great-Lordship is nothing but the reflexive-awareness — the one who is aware of himself,
fixedly, is the Lord; and that reflexive-awareness is the God's own pure knowledge-and-action. The
great-Lordship is not an added power; it is the self-awareness itself." (kārikā 11, V2S)
  • Why this is original.** The IPK states the three powers; Abhinava shows they reduce to the
  • lf-awareness, and that the Lordship is that self-awareness. The māheśvarya is not a fifth power; it is
  • at the four are. The Lord is not a being who has powers; he is the self-awareness the powers express.
  • The systematic gain.** This makes the recognition-thesis a metaphysics: the Lord = the self-awareness
  • the felt reflexivity of light. Recognition is the re-cognition of the self as this self-aware light.
  • e jñānādhikāra closes on this: the powers reduce to the self-awareness, and the self-awareness is the
  • rd.

5. The tattva-ontology and the soteriology (V3J–P)

  • e final regions are the ontology and the path.

5.1 The Śivatattva as the body of every category (V3J)

  • e āgamādhikāra supplies what reason cannot — the categories of the world, from the Lord's teaching,
  • cause "perception is not an omniscient eye; inference lacks the pervasion; only the āgama measures
  • e whole" (V3J). And its pivot:
"At the heart of it all is the Śivatattva, which is the body of every category... knowledge and
action — manifestation and reflexive-awareness — are un-joined, inseparable; and this inseparable
pair is the supreme form of all beings." (V3J)

5.2 The kañcukas and the malas (V3K/L)

  • e coverings (niyati, kāla, rāga, vidyā, kalā) hide the pure self in the bound state; the three stains
  • ṇava, māyīya, kārma) bind the knowers; the paśu (the bound one) and the pati (the Lord) define the
  • lation.

5.3 The jīvanmukta and the guru-paramparā (V3N–P)

  • e closing sum: the recognition as the path, the while-living-liberated (jīvanmukta), the transmission
  • om guru, śāstra, and self.
"Since liberation is from the recognition alone, all the elaborate effort-yogas are useless here;
this is the clear means, effort-less, un-undertaken, yet bearing the great fruit." (V3P)
  • d the lover-image closes the whole: "the world-Lord, always present, always near, is not experienced
  • his own splendor until the recognition arises" (V3P).

6. The map of Abhinava's original regions

  • Region | Locus | What it adds beyond the IPK |
  • -------|-------|------------------------------|
  • The epistemology of action | V3A–I | action = the will; causality = the knower's agency; inference across knowers; the anti-monist realism |
  • The sphurattā (the throbbing) | V2I | the reflexivity-claim made dynamic and felt |
  • The parā-vāk (the Word) | V2H/I | the reflexivity-claim identified with speech; language absorbed into recognition |
  • The māheśvarya (the Lordship) | V2R/S | the powers reduce to the self-awareness; the Lord = the self-awareness |
  • The tattva-ontology | V3J–M | the Śivatattva, the kañcukas, the malas, the categories |
  • The soteriology | V3N–P | the jīvanmukta, the guru-paramparā, the recognition-path |
  • The thesis.* Abhinava's original contribution is not a single new claim but the *completion of the
  • stem: the epistemology of action, the dynamic felt (sphurattā), the linguistic absorption (parā-vāk),
  • e reduction of the powers (māheśvarya), the ontology, and the soteriology. Utpaladeva states the seed;
  • hinava grows it into a complete metaphysics. These are the regions the recognition-thesis could not
  • ve without him, and they are the "goes further" territory of the authoritative source.
  • his is the extensions essay. Abhinava's four original regions: the epistemology of action (V3A–I,
  • e largest), the sphurattā (V2I), the parā-vāk (V2H/I), and the māheśvarya (V2R/S), plus the ontology
  • 3J–M) and the soteriology (V3N–P). These are what the IPVV adds beyond the IPK — the completion of
  • e system, the "goes further" territory.*
